bull2019.authors: Bull JR, Rowland SP, Scherwitzl EB, Scherwitzl R, Danielsson KG, Harper J
bull2019.title: Real-world menstrual cycle characteristics of more than 600,000 menstrual cycles
bull2019.finding: Mean cycle 29.3 days, follicular 16.9 (95% CI 10-30), luteal 12.4 (95% CI 7-17). Cycle length falls ~0.18 days per year of age from 25 to 45.

najmabadi2020.authors: Najmabadi S, Schliep KC, Simonsen SE, Porucznik CA, Egger MJ, Stanford JB
najmabadi2020.title: Menstrual bleeding, cycle length, and follicular and luteal phase lengths in women without known subfertility: a pooled analysis of three cohorts
najmabadi2020.finding: 581 women, 3,324 cycles. Menses 6.2 days, cycle 30.3 (median 29), follicular 18.5 (median 17), luteal 11.7 (median 12). Within-woman luteal length varied >3 days in 58.8% of women.

fehring2006.authors: Fehring RJ, Schneider M, Raviele K
fehring2006.title: Variability in the phases of the menstrual cycle
fehring2006.finding: 1,060 cycles: mean 28.9 days, 95% between 22 and 36. 42.5% of women varied >7 days. Only 25% had their whole fertile window between days 10 and 17. Follicular phase drives most variability.

mcnulty2020.authors: McNulty KL, Elliott-Sale KJ, Dolan E, Swinton PA, Ansdell P, Goodall S, Thomas K, Hicks KM
mcnulty2020.title: The effects of menstrual cycle phase on exercise performance in eumenorrheic women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
mcnulty2020.finding: 78 studies. Performance might be trivially reduced in the early follicular phase (ES -0.06). Too small and variable for general guidelines; a personalised approach is recommended.

colensosemple2023.authors: Colenso-Semple LM, D'Souza ACD, Elliott-Sale KJ, Phillips SM
colensosemple2023.title: Current evidence shows no influence of women's menstrual cycle phase on acute strength performance or adaptations to resistance exercise training
colensosemple2023.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
colensosemple2023.finding: Umbrella review: premature to conclude hormone fluctuations appreciably affect strength, performance or hypertrophy from resistance training.

armour2019cochrane.authors: Armour M, Ee CC, Naidoo D, Ayati Z, Chalmers KJ, Steel KA, de Manincor MJ, Delshad E
armour2019cochrane.title: Exercise for dysmenorrhoea
armour2019cochrane.finding: Exercise 45-60 min, 3+ times/week, any intensity, may reduce menstrual pain by ~25 mm on a 100 mm VAS. Low-quality evidence.

tsai2024.authors: Tsai IC, Hsu CW, Chang CH, Lei WT, Tseng PT, Chang KV
tsai2024.title: Comparative effectiveness of different exercises for reducing pain intensity in primary dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
tsai2024.finding: 29 RCTs, 1,808 participants. All exercise types reduced menstrual pain at 8 weeks; relaxation exercise most effective and lowest dropout.

armour2019selfcare.authors: Armour M, Smith CA, Steel KA, Macmillan F
armour2019selfcare.title: The effectiveness of self-care and lifestyle interventions in primary dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis
armour2019selfcare.finding: 23 trials, 2,302 women. Exercise large effect, heat and acupressure moderate. Exercise and heat more effective than analgesics for pain intensity.

jo2018.title: Heat therapy for primary dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis of its effects on pain relief and quality of life
jo2018.finding: 6 RCTs. Heating pads better than analgesics (SMD -0.72). Suggestive evidence, small trials.

daily2015.authors: Daily JW, Zhang X, Kim DS, Park S
daily2015.title: Efficacy of ginger for alleviating the symptoms of primary dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
daily2015.finding: 4 placebo RCTs: 750-2000 mg ginger powder in the first 3-4 days reduced pain. Suggestive evidence.

gorczyca2016.authors: Gorczyca AM, Sjaarda LA, Mitchell EM, Perkins NJ, Schliep KC, Wactawski-Wende J, Mumford SL
gorczyca2016.title: Changes in macronutrient, micronutrient, and food group intakes throughout the menstrual cycle in healthy, premenopausal women
gorczyca2016.finding: 259 women. Protein intake highest mid-luteal. Appetite and cravings for chocolate, sweets and salt higher in the late luteal phase.

davidsen2007.authors: Davidsen L, Vistisen B, Astrup A
davidsen2007.title: Impact of the menstrual cycle on determinants of energy balance: a putative role in weight loss attempts
davidsen2007.finding: Review: in the luteal phase energy intake and expenditure appear higher, with more cravings for high-carb and high-fat foods.

munro2023.authors: Munro MG, Mast AE, Powers JM, Kouides PA, O'Brien SH, Richards T, Lavin M, Levy BS
munro2023.title: The relationship between heavy menstrual bleeding, iron deficiency, and iron deficiency anemia
munro2023.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
munro2023.finding: Heavy menstrual bleeding is highly prevalent and a major contributor to iron deficiency and anaemia; often normalised by women and clinicians.

thysjacobs1998.authors: Thys-Jacobs S, Starkey P, Bernstein D, Tian J
thysjacobs1998.title: Calcium carbonate and the premenstrual syndrome: effects on premenstrual and menstrual symptoms
thysjacobs1998.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
thysjacobs1998.finding: 466 women, 1200 mg/day calcium for 3 cycles: 48% reduction in total symptom score vs 30% on placebo.

walker1998.authors: Walker AF, De Souza MC, Vickers MF, Abeyasekera S, Collins ML, Trinca LA
walker1998.title: Magnesium supplementation alleviates premenstrual symptoms of fluid retention
walker1998.finding: 38 women, 200 mg/day Mg: no effect in month 1; reduced fluid-retention symptoms (bloating, breast tenderness, swelling) in month 2.

romans2012.authors: Romans S, Clarkson R, Einstein G, Petrovic M, Stewart D
romans2012.title: Mood and the menstrual cycle: a review of prospective data studies
romans2012.finding: 47 studies: 38.3% found no mood-cycle link, only 14.9% linked negative mood to the premenstrual phase alone. No clear evidence of a premenstrual negative mood syndrome in the general population.

biggs2011.title: Premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder
biggs2011.finding: PMS affects 20-32% of premenopausal women, PMDD 3-8%. Limited evidence for calcium, vitamin D and B6.

baker2007.title: Circadian rhythms, sleep, and the menstrual cycle
baker2007.finding: Body temperature is higher in the luteal phase. Subjective sleep quality is lowest around menses; sleep timing and structure fairly stable otherwise.
